introduction-the-last-mile-of-machine-le.core: A model in a Jupyter notebook delivers no value. Serving is the 'last mile': packaging the model behind an API, scaling it, versioning it in a registry, and validating new versions safely in production.

first_principles.problem: A data scientist's 95%-accurate model never reaches users because nobody knows how to deploy it.
derivation: Test with **shadow mode**, then **A/B and canary**.

analogy.title: A chef's recipe vs. a restaurant
analogy.story: A great recipe in a notebook feeds nobody until the kitchen can cook it reliably for hundreds of diners.
analogy.breaks: Serving isn't the end. Monitoring for drift continues afterwards.

example.title: From notebook to production
example.outcome: you can see the path from notebook to production.

check.q: What is the 'last mile' of machine learning?
check.a: Getting a trained model into production behind reliable, scalable, versioned serving infrastructure.

inference-apis-how-apps-talk-to-models.core: Applications in any language call models through a standard API (REST/JSON for simplicity, gRPC for performance) with a clear request and response schema, versioning, timeouts and batching, so the model is a language-agnostic service.

first_principles.problem: A Python model can't be called directly from a JavaScript frontend or a Go backend.
derivation: Use **REST** for ease or **gRPC** for low latency/streaming.
Add **dynamic batching** to use GPUs efficiently.

analogy.title: A universal translator at a counter
analogy.story: Customers speaking any language get their order processed by the same kitchen.
analogy.breaks: Network hops add latency, so very low-latency cases may embed the model in-process.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any service can get a prediction.

check.q: Why use dynamic batching in inference servers?
check.a: Grouping concurrent requests into one batch uses GPUs much more efficiently, increasing throughput.

serving-tools-from-simple-to-supercharge.core: Serving options scale with needs: FastAPI wrappers for simple cases, model servers like TorchServe, Triton (multi-framework, dynamic batching, GPU sharing) and KServe/Seldon (Kubernetes-native, autoscaling, canaries), and LLM-specialised engines like vLLM and TGI.

first_principles.problem: A hand-written Flask app serving a GPU model can't batch, autoscale or roll out versions safely.
truths: Simple tools are fast to start.
Production serving needs batching, scaling and versioning.
derivation: **vLLM/TGI**: LLM serving with paged KV cache and continuous batching.

analogy.title: From a food stall to a restaurant chain
analogy.story: A stall works for a few customers; a chain needs standardised kitchens, logistics and quality control.
analogy.breaks: More powerful tools bring operational complexity, so match them to the need.

example.title: A KServe InferenceService

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An autoscaled endpoint with versioned storage.

code.text:
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: fraud }
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      modelFormat: { name: sklearn }
      storageUri: s3://models/fraud/v3

example.outcome: the right serving tool for each stage.

check.q: What special capability do LLM servers like vLLM add?
check.a: Efficient KV-cache memory management (PagedAttention) and continuous batching for high-throughput text generation.

the-model-registry-version-control-for-m.core: Git versions code but not multi-GB model artifacts or their lineage. A model registry (MLflow, SageMaker, W&B) stores versioned models with metadata: training data version, code commit, hyperparameters, metrics and stage (staging or production).

first_principles.problem: A model misbehaves in production, and nobody knows which data or code produced it or how to roll back.
truths: Models depend on code, data and parameters.
derivation: **Serve by version**; roll back by re-pointing.

analogy.title: A pharmacy's batch records
analogy.story: Every medicine batch records ingredients, process and tests, so a bad batch can be traced and recalled.
analogy.breaks: The registry is only as good as the metadata logged, so automate logging in training pipelines.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every production model is traceable and reversible.

code.text:
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_params(params); mlflow.log_metric("auc", 0.91)
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model", registered_model_name="fraud")
# later: client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud", "production", version=7)

check.q: Why isn't Git enough to version ML models?
check.a: Models are large binary artifacts whose behaviour depends on data and parameters that Git doesn't track.

testing-in-production-shadow-mode.core: Shadow mode sends real production requests to the new model in parallel with the current one, but only the current model's responses are returned to users. You compare predictions, latency and errors on real traffic with zero user risk.

first_principles.problem: A model that scores well offline may fail on real-world inputs, latency or edge cases.
truths: Offline test sets don't match live distributions.
derivation: **Compare** agreement, error rates and distribution shifts.
**Promote** only when the shadow looks healthy.

analogy.title: A trainee pilot shadowing in the cockpit
analogy.story: They make decisions alongside the real pilot without controlling the plane.
analogy.breaks: Shadow mode doubles inference cost and can't measure business outcomes (users never see the new results).

example.title: Shadowing a new fraud model
flow: v8 flags 3x more on a new merchant category

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A surprise is caught with no user impact.

check.q: What can't shadow mode tell you about a new model?
check.a: Its effect on business outcomes, because users never see the shadow model's predictions.

testing-in-production-ab-testing-and-can.core: Canary releases send a small share of real traffic to the new model to check technical safety. A/B tests split users between models to measure business impact (conversion, revenue) with statistical significance. Use both after shadow mode.

first_principles.problem: A technically accurate model might still hurt business metrics, such as more relevant but less profitable recommendations.
truths: Accuracy isn't the same as business value.
Statistics separate real effects from noise.
derivation: **Canary**: 1–5% of traffic, watch errors and latency.
**A/B**: randomise users, define the primary metric and sample size.
**Roll out** the winner, or roll back.

analogy.title: Taste-testing a new recipe
analogy.story: Serve it to a few tables first (canary), then compare sales of old vs new on similar nights (A/B).
analogy.breaks: A/B tests need enough traffic and time, and peeking early inflates false positives.

example.title: Recommendation model rollout
example.outcome: models promoted on evidence of value.

check.q: What's the difference between a canary release and an A/B test for models?
check.a: A canary checks technical safety on a small slice of traffic; an A/B test measures business impact with randomised groups and statistics.
